transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The White House is proposing a new set of tariffs on goods from 14 economies, including
China, Japan, Vietnam, South Korea, and the European Union.
The White House is also announcing modifications to earlier tariffs on Brazil.
On CNBC's Squawk Box, U.S. trade representative Jameson Greer frames the move as a response
to unfair trade practices.
So we're proposing, on the one part, targeted tariffs that apply to a subset of goods from
a given country at a tariff rate that maintains the deals we made with them.
And on the other hand, we're also negotiating with these countries.
We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity
and how to resolve it.
Mexico's not on the list.
Greer says the U.S. is still in trade talks with President Claudia Shambaugh's government.
After multiple delays, the army has blown up the national stockpile of lead azide in
Iowa.
This morning, the military carried out a controlled detonation of the degraded bomb-making materials
saying it was necessary, otherwise the material could have blown up uncontrollably as temperatures
cooled.
Now, on the eve of Thanksgiving, people are waiting to learn if the soil, air, or water
has been contaminated, officials took large amounts of samples before and after the detonation.
But hundreds of homes and farms could still be exposed to toxic dust particles.
We have more from NPR's Kat Von Storff.
Military explosive experts detonated more than 60 barrels of unstable lead azide at
the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middleton, Iowa.
The degraded bomb-making material had been stockpiled for nearly 20 years and was at
risk of spontaneous explosion.
The blast sent plumes of white smoke hundreds of feet into the air, which quickly dissipated
in the south-blowing wind.
Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe posted on social media that initial analysis from the federal
government after the blast indicated, quote, "mitigation measures appear to have been successful,
and the explosion was well-contained."
It could be several days before experts know whether or how much lead dust was released
into the surrounding environment.
Experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure.
Kat Von Storff, NPR News.
Before the operation, people were advised to evacuate to avoid breathing contaminated
air.
But shortly before the blast, about an hour before, the Federal Emergency Management Agency
advised those in a 20-mile radius of the blast to stay put for their safety.
In other news, for the first time, the Federal Communications Commission is clearing the
deployment of a constellation of AI data centers in space.
Today, FCC Chair Brendan Carr announced the agency was authorizing Elon Musk's SpaceX
to deploy up to a million orbital compute modules or satellites to process vast amounts
of data to be used on Earth.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
A 17-hour hostage crisis in Cartagena, Colombia, is over.
Here's John Otis.
Several explosions were heard early Wednesday morning, just before police and army troops
entered the supermarket, where armed men were holding the hostages.
President Abelardo de la Esprella described the kidnappers as common criminals, who took
refuge inside the supermarket after they failed to rob cash from an armored truck.
Speaking at a news conference, the president said one of the gunmen was killed after he
refused to release the hostages.
The kidnappings occurred as Colombians marked the 10th anniversary of a peace treaty that
disarmed the country's largest guerrilla group.
For NPR News, I'm John Otis in Bogota.
Titles banning music made entirely through generative AI.
Here's NPR's Chloe Veltman.
Tidal announced on social media that its ban on tracks created solely with AI will take
effect on December 9th, but tracks made with help from AI will still be permitted.
The company says over the past three months, more than 40 percent of all tracks on its
platforms are totally AI-generated, and that less than 5 percent of them receive even a
single stream.
Dan Macta is a managing director for Tidal Competitor Cobuz.
He says his company is also trying to figure out how to solve the AI slop problem, but
he says detecting and banning offending tracks is unlikely to work.
Because the AI will figure out how to create content that's not detectable.
Apple and Spotify still allow songs made completely with AI to appear on their platforms.
Chloe Veltman, NPR News.
This is NPR.

Army detonates national stockpile of degraded lead azide at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middleton
